Title: The effects of Kenya’s mining industry on women’s health and safety
NewsSummary: Harsh conditions impact the health and safety of women in artisanal and small-scale mining in Kenya.
NewsContent:
Although the extractives industry in Kenya is at an early stage, it can benefit local communities through job creation, livelihood improvement and enhanced infrastructure development. However, numerous human health challenges have emerged due to poor enforcement of mining policies and regulations, such as that of Kenya’s 2016 Mining Act. This legislation emphasises ‘Regulations for safety and health of persons employed in mines, and the carrying on of prospecting or mining operations in a safe, proper, sanitary and effectual manner’, but to this day this has not been implemented.

The lack of enforcement of laws in Kenya’s extractives sector has consequently threatened the health and safety status of women directly and indirectly involved in mining. This is especially the case in artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM).

The East Africa Institute’s (EAI) ‘Economy and Ecology’ programme area, which investigates the extractives sector in East Africa, aims to determine best practices to create a safe, inclusive and gender-balanced environment for women associated with the mining industry.

Thus, EAI is currently examining Kenya’s ASM industry and its impact on women directly and indirectly associated within this sector. This research specifically assesses the industry's impact on women’s health, as well as the social, economic and cultural obstacles they face. The findings will be used to bring about sustainable strategies to enforce women’s rights and overall well-being in ASM.

In Kasigau, an area located in Taita Taveta County, 20 percent of women work in ASM (Mwakumanya, Maghenda & Juma, 2016). These women primarily take on roles as casual workers in mining processing, mineral dealing and as agents or brokers. Not only do they work exhausting hours and are paid poorly (less than a dollar a day), they are regularly exposed to harsh physical mining conditions, adversely affecting their health and safety.

Women in the area are also exposed to waterborne diseases as they are surrounded by contaminated stagnant water in abandoned mining pits. This, in turn, limits the amount of drinking and bathing water available to them. Further, with a lack of occupational health and safety equipment and training, women are unable to protect themselves against toxic substance exposure, dust particles and occupational illnesses in general.

Sexual abuse and violence in many ASM communities such as Kasigau is another major challenge. There is often high criminal activity in abandoned mining areas, enhancing their susceptibility to sexual harassment and attacks. As a result, exposure to sexually transmitted infections and HIV/AIDS is high in these areas, impacting women’s sexual and reproductive health, as well as their psychological well-being (Mwakumanya et al., 2016).

With the lack of infrastructure in ASM areas, health and safety facilities are inaccessible as well as inadequate, further intensifying women’s physical and mental health risks.

To mitigate the impacts of ASM; general education, training and awareness-raising on related issues are essential in creating a safe, secure, inclusive and socially just environment for women associated with the mining industry in Kenya.

There is also a need to educate women on their human and mining rights to enable them to protect themselves. Having organised women’s groups for those involved in mining can help advocate for female empowerment in this sector and build up their capacity to create change. Training both men and women on occupational health and safety is also crucial in creating a safe and secure work environment.

Finally, it is crucial for not only Kenyan County governments but also influential agencies, such as UN Women Africa and UNDP, to take the lead in advocating for female empowerment in mining areas in Kenya and to enforce women’s rights in this sector.​


Rosie Jervase is an EAI Research Assistant, conducting research on women's health in Kenya's artisanal and small-scale mining sector.
